units.title: Studying Earth
units.blurb: Earth as a set of linked systems, and the maps that say where a place is and how high it stands.

units.title: Earth, Sun and Moon
units.blurb: How Earth's spin and orbit, and the Moon's orbit, make days, seasons, phases, eclipses and tides.

units.title: The Solar System and Beyond
units.blurb: What orbits the Sun, how big and far apart things are, and where the Sun sits among the stars and galaxies.

units.title: Inside Earth
units.blurb: Density, Earth's layers, and the slow flow of hot rock that moves the surface.

units.title: Minerals and Rocks
units.blurb: What minerals are, how to tell them apart, and how the three rock families form and turn into one another.

units.title: Weathering, Erosion and Soil
units.blurb: How rock breaks down, how soil forms, and how water, wind, ice and gravity carve and build landscapes over time.

units.title: Earth's History
units.blurb: Fossils, the rules for putting rock layers in order, radioactive clocks, and the geologic time scale.

units.title: Plate Tectonics
units.blurb: The evidence that continents move, the kinds of plate boundaries and what forms at each, and how fast plates go.

units.title: Earthquakes and Volcanoes
units.blurb: Seismic waves and how earthquakes are measured, kinds of volcanoes, hot spots, and forecasting natural hazards.

units.title: Water on Earth
units.blurb: Where Earth's water is, how sunlight and gravity move it around, and the water hidden underground.

units.title: Air and Weather
units.blurb: What the atmosphere is made of, how pressure and uneven heating make wind, global wind belts, and air masses and fronts.

units.title: Oceans and Climate
units.blurb: How winds and density move the ocean, what sets a place's climate, and the greenhouse effect and today's warming.

units.title: Resources and People
units.blurb: Where Earth's resources come from, and how the number of people and how much each uses add up to an impact.

topics.title: Earth's Four Spheres
topics.short: Sort the parts of Earth into geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere and biosphere, and spot where they interact.
topics.trouble: Students treat each sphere as separate and miss that most events, like rain washing soil into a river, involve two or more spheres at once.

topics.title: Latitude and Longitude
topics.short: Find any place on Earth by its degrees north or south of the equator and east or west of the prime meridian.
topics.trouble: Students swap latitude and longitude, or think lines of latitude meet at the poles, when it is lines of longitude that do.

topics.title: Reading Topographic Maps
topics.short: Read elevations from contour lines, and tell steep slopes from gentle ones and hills from valleys.
topics.trouble: Students read closely spaced contour lines as low or flat ground, when close lines mean a steep slope, or take a contour line for a road or a trail.

topics.title: Earth's Spin: Day and Night
topics.short: Earth turns once a day, so the Sun seems to rise in the east, cross the sky and set in the west.
topics.trouble: Students think the Sun travels around Earth each day, or that night comes when the Sun goes behind clouds or the Moon.

topics.title: Why We Have Seasons
topics.short: Earth's tilted axis changes the Sun's height in the sky and the length of the day through the year.
topics.trouble: Students say summer comes when Earth is closest to the Sun, yet Earth is closest in early January, during northern winter, and the two hemispheres have opposite seasons.

topics.title: Phases of the Moon
topics.short: Half the Moon is always lit by the Sun; as the Moon orbits Earth, we see different amounts of that lit half.
topics.trouble: Students think Earth's shadow makes the phases. Earth's shadow falls on the Moon only during a lunar eclipse.

topics.title: Solar and Lunar Eclipses
topics.short: An eclipse happens when the Sun, Earth and Moon line up, which the Moon's tilted orbit allows only a few times a year.
topics.trouble: Students expect an eclipse every month, missing that the Moon's orbit is tilted about 5° to Earth's, so most new and full moons pass just above or below the line-up.

topics.title: Gravity and Orbits
topics.short: Gravity pulls every mass toward every other mass; an orbit is falling around a body while moving sideways fast enough to keep missing it.
topics.trouble: Students believe there is no gravity in space, so astronauts float; in orbit they are falling around Earth together with their spacecraft.

topics.title: Tides
topics.short: The Moon's pull makes two bulges of ocean, so most coasts get two high tides and two low tides about every 24 hours 50 minutes.
topics.trouble: Students picture a single bulge facing the Moon and expect one high tide a day; there is a second bulge on the side of Earth away from the Moon.

topics.title: Planets, Moons and Small Bodies
topics.short: Tell the rocky inner planets from the giant outer planets, and place moons, dwarf planets, asteroids and comets.
topics.trouble: Students guess that Mercury is the hottest planet because it is closest to the Sun, but Venus is hotter, because its thick carbon dioxide air traps heat.

topics.title: The Scale of the Solar System
topics.short: Use astronomical units and scale models to see how small the planets are and how far apart they lie.
topics.trouble: Book pictures squeeze the planets together, so students think the planets are close to one another and nearly as big as the Sun.

topics.title: Light-Years, Stars and Galaxies
topics.short: A light-year is a distance; the Sun is one ordinary star among hundreds of billions in the Milky Way galaxy.
topics.trouble: Students think a light-year measures time, or that the stars lie just past the planets.

topics.title: Density
topics.short: Density is mass per volume; it decides what floats and what sinks, and how Earth sorted itself into layers.
topics.trouble: Students say heavy things sink and light things float, mixing up mass with density; a huge log floats while a small pebble sinks.

topics.title: Earth's Layers
topics.short: The crust, mantle, outer core and inner core differ in what they are made of, how dense they are and whether they are solid or liquid.
topics.trouble: Students picture the mantle as a sea of liquid magma, but it is nearly all solid rock that creeps very slowly; only the outer core is liquid.

topics.title: Lithosphere and Asthenosphere
topics.short: The rigid lithosphere, the crust plus the top of the mantle, rides on the hot, softer asthenosphere below.
topics.trouble: Students think the plates are only the crust, or that they float on liquid; plates include the top of the mantle and slide over hot, weak but solid rock.

topics.title: Convection
topics.short: Warm fluid expands, becomes less dense and rises while cooler, denser fluid sinks, making a loop.
topics.trouble: Students say "heat rises" as if heat were a substance; warm fluid rises because the denser, cooler fluid around it sinks and pushes it up.

topics.title: What Makes a Mineral
topics.short: A mineral is a natural, inorganic solid with a definite chemical makeup and an orderly crystal structure.
topics.trouble: Students call any rock, gem or crystal a mineral, and are surprised that ice counts while glass and coal do not.

topics.title: Identifying Minerals
topics.short: Use hardness, streak, luster, cleavage and density to identify a mineral, since color can fool you.
topics.trouble: Students identify minerals by color, though one mineral can come in many colors, and read Mohs hardness 10 as ten times harder than 1 when the scale is only a ranking.

topics.title: Igneous Rocks
topics.short: Igneous rock forms when melted rock cools; slow cooling underground grows large crystals, and fast cooling at the surface makes small ones.
topics.trouble: Students expect fast cooling to make big crystals, when crystals need time to grow; lava that cools in seconds can even become glass.

topics.title: Sedimentary Rocks
topics.short: Sediments settle in layers, then are pressed together and cemented into rock; rocks made of grains are named by grain size.
topics.trouble: Students think sediment turns into rock just by drying out, missing the squeezing by layers piled on top and the natural cement that glues the grains.

topics.title: Metamorphic Rocks
topics.short: Heat and pressure change a rock's minerals and texture without melting it.
topics.trouble: Students think metamorphic rock forms by melting; if a rock melts, it becomes magma and cools into igneous rock.

topics.title: The Rock Cycle
topics.short: Any rock can become any other kind through melting, weathering, burial, heat and pressure, driven by Earth's inner heat and the Sun.
topics.trouble: Students learn the cycle as one fixed loop, igneous to sedimentary to metamorphic, but rocks can skip steps or go another way, as when metamorphic rock weathers straight into sediment.

topics.title: Mechanical and Chemical Weathering
topics.short: Rock breaks into smaller pieces (mechanical weathering) or changes into new substances (chemical weathering).
topics.trouble: Students mix up weathering, the breaking down of rock in place, with erosion, the carrying away of the pieces.

topics.title: What Speeds Up Weathering
topics.short: More surface area, more water and warmth, and minerals that break down easily make rock weather faster.
topics.trouble: Students don't expect breaking a rock to expose more surface: one 2 cm cube has 24 cm² of surface, but cut into eight 1 cm cubes it has 48 cm².

topics.title: How Soil Forms
topics.short: Soil is weathered rock mixed with water, air and living and once-living matter, built up slowly in layers called horizons.
topics.trouble: Students think soil is just dirt that was always there, not a mixture that forms over centuries or longer from rock, water, air and living things.

topics.title: Erosion and Deposition
topics.short: Water, wind, ice and gravity carry sediment away and drop it where they slow down.
topics.trouble: Students think erosion only destroys land, missing that every grain carried away is set down somewhere, building deltas, beaches and dunes.

topics.title: Landforms Made by Water, Wind and Ice
topics.short: Read a landscape: V-shaped valleys and deltas from rivers, U-shaped valleys and moraines from glaciers, dunes from wind.
topics.trouble: Students expect glacier deposits to be sorted by size like river deposits, but ice drops boulders, sand and clay together in one jumble.

topics.title: Slow and Fast Changes
topics.short: Tiny changes each year add up over millions of years, while a few changes, like landslides, happen in minutes.
topics.trouble: Students can't picture tiny yearly changes adding up, so they think big landforms like canyons must come from a single sudden event.

topics.title: Fossils
topics.short: Fossils are remains or traces of past life, usually kept when remains are buried quickly in sediment.
topics.trouble: Students think most living things become fossils; only a tiny share do, mostly ones with hard parts that were buried quickly.

topics.title: Superposition: Reading Layers in Order
topics.short: In layers that have not been disturbed, the oldest is at the bottom and the youngest is at the top.
topics.trouble: Students apply "oldest at the bottom" to layers that were later folded or flipped, where the order can be upside down.

topics.title: Cross-Cutting Relationships
topics.short: A fault or a body of igneous rock that cuts through other rock is younger than the rock it cuts.
topics.trouble: Students date an igneous dike by the layer where it ends, instead of seeing that it must be younger than every layer it cuts across.

topics.title: Half-Life and Absolute Age
topics.short: Radioactive atoms decay at a steady rate, so the fraction left tells a rock's age in years.
topics.trouble: Students think all the atoms are gone after two half-lives, but each half-life halves what is left: after two, one quarter remains.

topics.title: The Geologic Time Scale
topics.short: Earth's 4.6-billion-year history is divided into eons, eras and periods, marked by big changes in life.
topics.trouble: Students think people lived alongside dinosaurs; the last dinosaurs other than birds died about 66 million years ago, and our species appeared about 300,000 years ago.

topics.title: The Evidence for Moving Continents
topics.short: Matching coastlines, fossils, rock layers and scratches from ancient ice show the continents were once joined.
topics.trouble: Students think only the continents move, plowing through the ocean floor; whole plates move, ocean floor and all.

topics.title: Seafloor Spreading
topics.short: New ocean floor forms at mid-ocean ridges, so the rock gets older the farther it lies from a ridge.
topics.trouble: Students expect the ocean floor to hold Earth's oldest rock, but almost all of it is younger than about 200 million years, while some continental rock is about 4 billion years old.

topics.title: Three Kinds of Plate Boundaries
topics.short: Plates pull apart at divergent boundaries, push together at convergent ones and slide past each other at transform ones.
topics.trouble: Students think plates moving apart leave an open gap; new rock fills a divergent boundary while old rock sinks at convergent ones, so Earth stays the same size.

topics.title: What Forms at Each Boundary
topics.short: Match ridges, rift valleys, trenches, volcanic arcs, mountain ranges and long faults to the boundaries that make them.
topics.trouble: Students think all mountains are volcanoes, but ranges like the Himalayas are crust crumpled where two continents collide.

topics.title: How Fast Plates Move
topics.short: Plates move a few centimeters a year, which adds up to hundreds of kilometers over millions of years.
topics.trouble: Students lose track of units: 5 cm a year for 2 million years is 10 million cm, which is 100 km, not 10 million km.

topics.title: Earthquakes and Seismic Waves
topics.short: Rock snaps along a fault and sends out P waves first, then S waves, then slower surface waves.
topics.trouble: Students think the epicenter is where the rock breaks; the break starts at the focus underground, and the epicenter is the point on the surface right above it.

topics.title: Earthquake Magnitude
topics.short: Each step up in magnitude means waves 10 times taller on a seismogram and about 32 times more energy.
topics.trouble: Students read magnitude like ordinary counting, so a magnitude 6 seems twice a magnitude 3, when its waves are 1,000 times taller and it releases about 30,000 times the energy.

topics.title: Kinds of Volcanoes
topics.short: Runny, low-silica lava builds broad shield volcanoes; sticky, gas-rich magma builds steep cones and erupts explosively.
topics.trouble: Students think lava flows are the main danger, but fast clouds of hot ash and gas (pyroclastic flows) and volcanic mudflows (lahars) have killed far more people.

topics.title: Hot Spots and Island Chains
topics.short: A plate sliding over a fixed hot spot leaves a line of volcanoes that get older with distance, which shows the plate's speed.
topics.trouble: Students assume every volcano sits on a plate boundary; Hawaii's volcanoes are in the middle of the Pacific Plate.

topics.title: Forecasting Natural Hazards
topics.short: Records and warning signs tell where hazards strike and how often, even when the exact day can't be known.
topics.trouble: Students believe scientists can predict the exact day of an earthquake; no one can yet, so forecasts give the chance of a quake over years or decades.

topics.title: Where Earth's Water Is
topics.short: About 97% of Earth's water is salty ocean; most fresh water is frozen in ice or held underground.
topics.trouble: Students think most fresh water is in lakes and rivers, but they hold well under 1% of it; most fresh water is ice and groundwater.

topics.title: The Water Cycle
topics.short: Energy from the Sun lifts water by evaporation, and gravity brings it back down as precipitation and runoff.
topics.trouble: Students think clouds are made of water vapor; vapor is invisible, and clouds are tiny drops of liquid water or ice crystals.

topics.title: Groundwater and Aquifers
topics.short: Rain soaks into spaces in soil and rock; below the water table they are full, and wells draw water from aquifers.
topics.trouble: Students picture groundwater as underground lakes and rivers, but it mostly fills tiny spaces between grains, and they mix up porosity (how much space) with permeability (how easily water flows).

topics.title: What Air Is Made Of
topics.short: Dry air is about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen and 1% argon, with small but important amounts of carbon dioxide.
topics.trouble: Students think air is mostly oxygen, or that carbon dioxide is a large part of it; carbon dioxide is about 0.04% of the air.

topics.title: Layers of the Atmosphere
topics.short: Temperature falls, rises, falls and rises again with height, marking the troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere and thermosphere.
topics.trouble: Students expect it to get colder all the way up; ozone warms the stratosphere, and the thin thermosphere is very hot.

topics.title: Air Pressure
topics.short: Air has weight, so it presses on everything around it; pressure is highest at sea level and drops as you go up.
topics.trouble: Students think air weighs nothing or that air pressure only pushes down; it pushes in every direction, and the air and fluids inside us push back just as hard, which is why we don't feel crushed.

topics.title: Wind and Local Breezes
topics.short: Uneven heating makes differences in pressure, and air flows from high to low pressure, as in sea breezes by day and land breezes at night.
topics.trouble: Students name a wind by where it is going; a north wind blows from the north.

topics.title: Global Winds and the Coriolis Effect
topics.short: Earth's spin bends moving air, turning the rising and sinking air of the tropics and poles into the trade winds, westerlies and polar easterlies.
topics.trouble: Students think the Coriolis effect makes sinks drain in opposite directions in the two hemispheres; it is far too weak at that size and matters only for large, long-lasting motions.

topics.title: Air Masses and Fronts
topics.short: Large bodies of air take on the warmth and moisture of where they formed; where two meet, a front brings a change in weather.
topics.trouble: Students think warm and cold air mix right away at a front; the denser cold air stays low and wedges under the warm air, lifting it, which makes the clouds.

topics.title: Surface Ocean Currents
topics.short: Steady winds drive surface currents into giant loops that carry warm water toward the poles and cool water toward the equator.
topics.trouble: Students think tides or the Moon drive ocean currents; surface currents are pushed mainly by steady winds and turned by Earth's spin.

topics.title: Deep Ocean Currents
topics.short: Cold, salty water is dense and sinks near the poles, driving a slow current that winds through every ocean.
topics.trouble: Students think salt makes water lighter, or that the deep ocean sits still; cold, salty water is the densest, and it slowly flows along the bottom around the globe.

topics.title: Weather and Climate
topics.short: Weather is the state of the air at a time and place; climate is the pattern of weather over 30 years or more.
topics.trouble: Students treat one cold week as evidence against a warming climate, mixing up a few days of weather with long-term averages.

topics.title: What Sets a Place's Climate
topics.short: Latitude, elevation, distance from the sea, ocean currents and mountains together set a region's climate.
topics.trouble: Students expect places at the same latitude to share a climate, missing the effect of ocean currents, elevation and mountains; London has far milder winters than Calgary, at nearly the same latitude.

topics.title: The Greenhouse Effect
topics.short: Sunlight warms the ground, the ground gives off infrared light, and greenhouse gases absorb some of it and send part back down.
topics.trouble: Students confuse the greenhouse effect with the ozone hole, or think greenhouse gases trap incoming sunlight; they absorb the infrared that the warmed Earth gives off.

topics.title: Evidence of a Warming World
topics.short: Thermometer records, rising seas, shrinking ice and the rising carbon dioxide record show that Earth has warmed over the last century.
topics.trouble: Students judge the trend from one hot or cold year, but years bounce up and down; the warming shows in averages over decades, more than 1 °C since the late 1800s.

topics.title: Renewable and Nonrenewable Resources
topics.short: Some resources renew within a human lifetime; others, like fossil fuels and metal ores, took millions of years to form where they are.
topics.trouble: Students think resources are spread evenly or that groundwater always refills quickly; ores, oil and good aquifers lie only where past geologic processes put them, and some aquifers take thousands of years to refill.

topics.title: People and Earth's Systems
topics.short: Total use equals the number of people times the use per person, so growth in either one raises the impact.
topics.trouble: Students blame impact on population alone, or on consumption alone; the total depends on both, multiplied together.
